summary:
We developed an educational website dedicated to spacecraft and rovers. It’s written for children aged 5 to 10. NASA data was used to present accurate and interesting information about the rovers and explain what they did to study these planets.

By bringing these missions together, we aim to show that a spacecraft does not become unimportant when its mission ends. Remembering these missions helps us understand how modern lunar exploration was built and why every step of space exploration matters.
details:
Our project is about inviting the younger generation to take interest in space, exploration programs, and historical missions.

We wrote all the text for kids aged 5 to 10, so it stays fun and easy to follow. Kids start by picking their travel destination, the Moon or Mars. On each page they explore the real equipment that was left there: the Lunar Module, the Laser Ranging Retroreflector and the SIDE experiment on the Moon, and the Spirit & Opportunity rovers and the Ingenuity helicopter on Mars. Every machine is an interactive picture. Kids hover over or tap a part, like the rover’s rocker-bogie wheels or its camera head, and it lights up and explains what it did. The Mars page also has a mission map with pins that show where each mission landed.

Our website is dyslexia friendly, and we achieved that by using the Lexend Exa font, making sure that it's easier to read. We also added alt text to every image, so screen readers can describe it.

Our website also works on mobile, so every kid can enjoy a little learning everywhere!

We used AI to help generate the HTML5, CSS and JavaScript. We designed the site, wrote the content, and tested and adjusted everything ourselves.
We tested it on Windows 11 and Linux Debian in Chrome and Zen Browser, and on Android in Chrome.
For text & code editing, we used Notepad++ and Kate, and our website is hosted on InfinityFree.

Our project is creative because it turns old, “abandoned” machines into stories kids can explore themselves. Instead of reading long paragraphs, they discover each part by touching it, under a starry sky that changes on every visit. We kept rethinking and rebuilding parts of the site until they suited kids and were still fun to read and interact with.

We know not everyone reads the same way, so accessibility came first: the dyslexia-friendly font was our first decision, then screen reader support.


Our project's repository is on GitHub.
